That's tier 1-ish but narrow scope with contestation. Political intimidation of advocates is local-sphere mostly.

The facility restriction is a real universal-exposure-ish item but limited to one chain. Political violence against trans advocates is societal hostility, documented pattern. I'll go 0.72.

No criminalisation of same-sex conduct, no trans legal framework, no LGR (resident gap — don't deduct unless reaching visitors), no anti-discrimination statute, societal stigma documented but dated (2011/2012), 2018 NGO statement of some violence cases. General security context: 2012 coup, arbitrary killings, torture, impunity, drug-trafficking corruption — general crime, out of scope unless it undermines police protection. Actually a state with documented security-force torture and impunity, plus no protections for LGBT people, plus no data — this affects rule of law: no recourse. Thin data, structural signals: no anti-discrimination law, no LGR, no LGBT scene, poor travel safety, stigma, coup/impunity context. Rule of law weak → recourse thin.

Rule 13/22: thin dossier extrapolates from structural facts. No criminalisation is a plus. No trans-specific targeting documented. But governance character: arbitrary killings, torture, impunity, poor safety score. That's general crime — out of scope mostly, but signals collapse of protection. Hmm, but also note: no LGR means visitor's home passport is used anyway — neutral. No anti-discrimination statute = resident gap. Stigma = tier 3. Weak rule of law = recourse thin. I'll go 0.50.

Dossier 3: South Africa-like. Strong constitutional equality, Equality Court, hate crimes act 2024, LGR (resident), binding precedent protecting trans inmates (2025), documented violence against trans people in townships (five LGBTQIA+ murders Dec 2024 raw count; tavern assault Dec 2024 with arrest), documented police mockery/denial of service (2024 trans woman refused help filing DV case), academic finding that facility access lacks equal protection in practice. Border documentation unresolved (open question, light). Public opinion comparatively favorable (72% backing trans rights in 2017).

So: strong legal framework with documented operating remedies (court orders, prosecutions), but documented societal violence with thin township recourse and documented police mistreatment of a trans person. Precedence ladder worst feature: tier 3 (documented societal hostility with thin recourse in townships) plus documented police failure (mocking, refusing to take a DV report) — that's borderline tier 2. But there's also facility access unequal in practice (academic) — not established as a rule. Compared to calibration 0.65-A/B/C/D/E: they have some friction and uneven remedies. Five LGBTQIA+ murders in a month nationally, no denominator; general homicide in such a country is high. So background-ish. Police mockery incident is single. Strong protections documented as working (Nov 2025 ruling orders implementation).

I'd rate 0.68. Considering the mean subnational: townships violent, care concentrated in cities; visitors usually go to cities. Here: documented severe societal hostility (93%), religious leaders calling for killing, no community infrastructure, no recourse (no anti-discrimination, no orgs).

Dossier 5 has: one trans conviction 2021, one 2010, police arbitrary arrests documented in a 45-person study, forced stripping/exams, moratorium annulled. Enforcement "arbitrary and violent." Recent constitutional ruling (2024) removing any doubt. Outed visitor who's read as same-sex-conduct — a trans woman with a male partner would be squarely covered.

I'd rate 0.20. Severity ladder: imprisonment for 8 years, men's prison, sexual violence risk. Frequency: documented pattern of arbitrary arrests of trans people (2018 study), though enforcement contested. State hostile. 0.20 seems fair — High Risk band boundary. Maybe 0.19-0.22. I'll say 0.21.
